diagnostic_evidence.quote: the control-to-state map $\varepsilon \mapsto c(\,\cdot\, ,T; \varepsilon)$ is not convex
This is the reason why Theorem \ref{thm:saddle_point} is fundamental: it ensures that there is no duality gap.

issues.failure_explanation: Theorem 3.2 only says that the quadratic functional J has a unique minimiser over all of H^1(Omega) (the solution of an elliptic Neumann problem). The Mayer problem (OCP) minimises J(c(.,T;eps)) over eps in the admissible set, where u = c(.,T;eps) ranges over a nonconvex reachable set produced by a nonlinear ODE. No existence of an optimal control is proved. With a nonlinear dependence on eps and no convexity of velocity sets, weak-* compactness of the controls does not give it. The paper itself says only local minimisers can be expected. In the same way, Theorem 4.2 concerns L over free (u,v,mu), yet it is invoked to assert 'no duality gap' for the saddle problem (OCP_TV), whose primal variable is constrained to the nonconvex reachable set.

failure_location.quote: The following result ensures the well-posedness of the problem

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State that Theorem 3.2 concerns only the unconstrained functional J, and drop or weaken the claims of well-posedness of the control problem and of no duality gap for (OCP_TV). Alternatively, prove existence of an optimal control under extra hypotheses.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised well-posedness of the optimal control problems (Mayer and TV saddle versions) is not established. The 'no duality gap' justification of the ADMM stopping rule is unsupported.
issues.title: Results for free u in H^1 are claimed to give well-posedness of the control problem and no duality gap for the ADMM control problem
issues.why_classification: The least adequate repair withdraws a promised well-posedness result (a limited weakening). No new global argument is needed for the algorithms, but the theory gap is real.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we use the discrete functional gradient

issues.failure_explanation: In the appendix the variation of the augmented functional contains lambda(T)v(T) + [-Delta c(T) + alpha(c(T)-I)]v(T). Setting it to zero for arbitrary v(T) gives lambda(T) = Delta c(T) - alpha(c(T)-I), the opposite of the stated terminal condition. Likewise the derivation gives dJ/d(eps)[z] = -int lambda dF/d(eps) z, so the functional gradient should be minus the quantity declared as the 'discrete functional gradient'. The two sign errors cancel only if one silently redefines lambda. The text never says so, so the stated system does not follow from its derivation.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Fix one consistent sign convention: either lambda(T) = Delta c - alpha(c-I) with gradient -int lambda dF/d(eps), or redefine lambda -> -lambda in the Lagrangian. Then restate the terminal conditions (including eq:new_adjoint) and the discrete gradient accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The stated optimality system, the adjoint sign convention used in D = dF/d(eps).lambda, and the sign logic of the descent direction are not consistent with the derivation. The ADMM adjoint (eq:new_adjoint) inherits the same convention.
issues.title: Sign of the adjoint terminal condition (and of the discrete gradient) contradicts the appendix derivation
issues.why_classification: A local sign fix preserves the method and all claims; no new argument is needed.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: respectively on the lower and upper active contact sets

issues.failure_explanation: All Armijo tests evaluate J at Pi_E(eps - tau D) with sufficient decrease c tau |D|^2, so D is treated as the gradient and -D as the descent direction. The Remark's optimality inequalities (D>=0 on lower bounds, D<=0 on upper bounds) also treat D as the gradient. The final update, however, moves to Pi_E(eps + sigma D), a different point (ascent direction) for which the step size was never validated. The accepted step therefore carries no decrease guarantee, and the iteration actually ascends J.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use the same direction in the line search and the update, for example eps^{(j+1)} = Pi_E(eps^{(j)} - sigma^{(j+1)} D^{(j)}).
issues.overall_effect: As written, DAL does not implement steepest descent. Algorithm 2 reuses DAL for the u-step, so it is affected as well.
issues.title: DAL line search tests the step eps - tau D but the update uses eps + sigma D
issues.why_classification: A one-sign local correction restores the intended algorithm and all claims.

issues.failure_explanation: In the ELSE branch the initial step satisfies the Armijo condition, and tau is multiplied by 1/b while the condition still holds. The loop exits at the first tau^{(k)} for which the condition fails. The algorithm then sets sigma^{(j+1)} = tau^{(k)}, a step that violates sufficient decrease. The last admissible value is tau^{(k-1)}. In the backtracking branch the returned tau^{(k)} does satisfy the condition, so the two branches are inconsistent.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Return the last admissible step (tau^{(k-1)}, or b*tau^{(k)}) in the increase branch.
issues.overall_effect: The monotone-descent property that the Armijo rule is meant to guarantee is lost whenever the step is enlarged.
issues.title: Step-size increase branch of the two-way Armijo search returns a step that violates the Armijo condition
issues.why_classification: A routine local change to the returned step restores the guarantee without altering the method.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the compactly supported interaction kernel is given by the $C^2$ Wendland function

issues.failure_explanation: For the formula as given, phi(0) = -1 and phi(r) < 0 on [0,1/4). In the dynamics dot c_i = (1/N) sum phi(r_ij)(c_j - c_i), nearby, similar agents would then repel instead of align. This contradicts the intended consensus/clustering dynamics, the positivity phi > 0 needed for 'global interactions' in the Remark, and the positivity assumed in the opinion-dynamics results the paper cites. The function is also not the C^2 Wendland function it is said to be (whose factor is (4r+1)).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace (4r-1) by (4r+1), the standard C^2 Wendland function, and confirm the positivity of phi on [0,1).
issues.overall_effect: The kernel used to describe the simulations is incompatible with the model's stated behaviour. The derivative formulas, which use phi', would be applied to a repulsive kernel.
issues.title: Interaction kernel formula has the wrong sign and is negative (repulsive) for r < 1/4
issues.why_classification: A local, forced correction of the kernel formula leaves all claims intact.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: There exists a saddle point for the functional
The ensemble of these properties is sufficient to guarantee the existence of a saddle point in our setting

issues.failure_explanation: L has only linear growth in the gradient through |v|. For mu = 0 and v = grad u, L equals the ROF functional K, which stays bounded along smoothed step functions u_n with ||u_n||_{H^1} -> infinity. So L is not coercive on H^1 x L^2, and the 'as in Theorem 3.2' argument fails. A saddle point forces v* = grad u* in L^2, so u* would be an H^1 minimiser of K. For discontinuous data in L^2 (for instance I = indicator of a disc with alpha large) the ROF minimiser has a jump and is not in H^1, so the infimum over H^1 is not attained and no saddle point exists in the stated spaces. The dual side is also unaddressed: L is linear in mu and not coercive in the dual variable, but the cited saddle-point theorem needs dual-side conditions.

failure_location.quote: it is immediate to show coercivity in the primal variables, ensuring that the minimum is attained in a weakly compact set

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the theorem in a setting where it holds: the discrete finite-dimensional problem, or BV with a measure-valued v, or add regularity assumptions. Then supply compactness and duality arguments (for example Fenchel-Rockafellar duality) for it.
issues.overall_effect: Existence of a saddle point and strong duality are not established in the stated function spaces. The statement is false for edge-containing images in the continuous setting that motivates TV regularisation.
issues.title: Saddle-point existence proof uses false H^1 x L^2 coercivity and unverified hypotheses; the statement fails for discontinuous I
issues.why_classification: The numerics are discrete and survive. Repair needs a contained new argument or a restricted setting, with a recognisably comparable result.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In general, the saddle point is not unique.

issues.failure_explanation: At a saddle point (u*,v*,mu*), L(x*,mu) <= L(x*,mu*) holds for every mu once v* = grad u*. But the other inequality, L(x*,mu*) <= L(x,mu*) for all primal x, requires (u*,v*) to minimise L(.,.,mu*). This gives the first-order condition 0 in d|v*| + mu* + rho(v* - grad u*), i.e. mu* in -d|v*|, so |mu*| <= 1 a.e. and mu* = -v*/|v*| where v* != 0. For example, a constant mu of norm 10 is not a dual solution. The multiplier set is a constrained set, not all of L^2.

failure_location.quote: so that any $\mu \in L^2(\Omega; \R^2)$ becomes feasible

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the argument by the correct characterisation of optimal multipliers via the subdifferential of |.| (mu* in -d|v*|), and state that they are generally non-unique only where v* = 0.
issues.overall_effect: The stated reason for non-uniqueness of the dual part of the saddle point is wrong. The remark that the algorithms converge 'to one of the optimal dual ones' rests on a false characterisation of the dual set.
issues.title: Incorrect justification of non-uniqueness of the saddle point ('any mu becomes feasible')
issues.why_classification: It is a side remark. A local rewrite keeps the theorem and the algorithms unchanged.
